profile.name: Kshitiz Neupane
profile.intro: I study Computer Science and Mathematics at the University of Southern Mississippi. My work focuses on machine learning and data science.
profile.about: I am a student passionate about machine learning and artificial intelligence, with a particular interest in understanding and improving these fields through their mathematical foundations. I enjoy learning concepts from the ground up—digging into where ideas come from, why they work, and how they can be developed further through research. My goal is not only to use existing AI systems, but to contribute to the theory and methods behind them. Outside academics and research, I enjoy playing music, especially piano, and staying active through sports, particularly badminton. I see myself as a curious learner who enjoys exploring ideas deeply, building new things, and continuously challenging my understanding.

projects.name: ShiftGuard
projects.description: I built ShiftGuard to explore whether changes in incoming data can warn us that a model is becoming less reliable. It compares several ways of measuring those changes.
projects.resume_title: ShiftGuard — Model Failure Under Distribution Shift
bullets: Built a reproducible benchmark spanning 3 datasets, 5 classifiers, and 5 seeds, producing 12,000 model-window evaluations to compare Wasserstein, KL, PSI, and MMD as label-free failure signals.
Measured an overall failure ROC-AUC of 0.799 for maximum marginal Wasserstein (95% CI: 0.760–0.832); used validation-only calibration and documented variation across datasets and shift types.
projects.image_alt: Failure detection ROC curves from the full ShiftGuard experiment.
projects.caption: Failure detection ROC curves from the full ShiftGuard experiment.
projects.question: Can distribution shift warn us before a classifier fails?
details: ShiftGuard studies a practical problem: a model can look healthy when it is deployed even while the data it receives is changing. I built a repeatable experiment to test whether those changes can act as an early warning.

The project compares several distance measures across different datasets, classifiers, and types of shift. It also looks at false alarms and warning time, because a signal is only useful when it gives a clear and timely warning.
highlights: Compares Wasserstein distance, KL divergence, PSI, and MMD
Tests controlled and time-based changes in data
Measures warning quality as well as model performance

projects.name: F1 Race Analysis
projects.description: I use historical Formula 1 data to explore pit stops and predict race outcomes. The prediction models use information available before a race, such as qualifying and recent form.
bullets: Engineered pre-race features and reusable preprocessing/model pipelines, achieving holdout podium ROC-AUC of 0.943 and finish-position MAE of 3.554; excluded in-race variables from predictive inputs.
projects.image_alt: Yearly average pit-stop duration by team, exported from the F1 analysis notebook.
projects.caption: Yearly average pit-stop duration by team, exported from the F1 analysis notebook.
projects.question: What can we learn about race outcomes before the lights go out?
details: This project uses historical Formula 1 data to study race performance from two angles. One part looks at pit-stop patterns and team differences. The other builds models that estimate finishing position and podium chances before a race starts.
I kept pre-race prediction separate from the pit-stop analysis so information from the race itself does not leak into the predictions. The work includes reusable data preparation and model pipelines.
highlights: Explores pit-stop performance across teams and seasons
Uses qualifying, grid position, and recent form for prediction
Keeps analysis variables separate from pre-race model inputs

projects.name: Bayesian Linear Regression
projects.description: A hands-on study of Bayesian regression using housing data. I look at both the predicted prices and the uncertainty around them.
projects.image_alt: Posterior predictive means and ±2σ bands from the California Housing notebook.
projects.caption: Posterior predictive means and ±2σ bands from the California Housing notebook.
projects.question: A prediction is only part of the answer. How uncertain is it?
projects.result: Closed-form posterior · Predictive uncertainty · Residual diagnostics
details: I built this project to understand linear regression as a probability model rather than only a line-fitting method. It starts with a Gaussian likelihood and prior, then works through MAP estimation and the full posterior using the California Housing dataset.

The notebook studies how prior choices affect coefficients and how uncertainty in those coefficients becomes uncertainty in a prediction. Residual plots are used to see where the simple model still falls short.
highlights: Implements MAP estimation directly with NumPy
Shows posterior uncertainty for model coefficients
Builds prediction intervals and checks residual patterns

projects.name: PCA from Scratch
projects.description: I built PCA from the underlying linear algebra to understand how it compresses handwritten digit images. I explore what information stays and what gets lost.
projects.image_alt: MNIST digits projected onto the first two principal components.
projects.caption: MNIST digits projected onto the first two principal components.
projects.question: How much structure survives when we reduce the dimensions?
details: This project builds principal component analysis from its linear algebra. I use handwritten digits to see how covariance, eigenvectors, and maximum-variance directions turn a large image space into a smaller representation.

The visualizations show the first two components, the patterns learned by the components, and how well digits can be rebuilt after compression. This makes the tradeoff between fewer dimensions and lost detail visible.
highlights: Implements PCA from covariance and eigendecomposition
Projects MNIST digits into two dimensions
Measures and visualizes reconstruction quality

projects.name: ManageYourHome
projects.description: An app for keeping track of shared household purchases. It works out each person’s share and keeps expenses in one place.
projects.result: JWT authentication · Shared expense calculations · REST API
bullets: Built a full-stack expense-sharing app with JWT access-token refresh, authenticated CRUD APIs, pagination, and server-side per-user expense and tax calculations.
projects.image_alt: Local application screenshot of the shared expense list.
projects.caption: Local application screenshot of the shared expense list.
projects.question: Making shared household expenses easier to understand.
details: ManageYourHome helps people record purchases made for a household and divide the cost among the people who share them. Each list keeps the items, tax, payer, and individual shares together.

The application has a React and TypeScript interface backed by a Django REST API. It includes authentication, editable lists, per-person totals, and a details view for reviewing spending across several lists.
highlights: Calculates item shares and tax on the server
Supports secure sign-in and editable expense lists
Shows spending totals by person and category

projects.question: Connecting everyday transactions to a clearer budget.
details: Money Manager is a personal budgeting application for recording income and expenses, setting a monthly budget, and reviewing spending over time.

The application uses Kivy for its interface and SQLite for local storage. It can also run through Docker with a browser-based display, which makes the desktop application easier to try on another computer.
highlights: Records income and expense transactions
Tracks monthly budgets and spending summaries
Stores data locally with SQLite
